findings.title: Bare except with unguarded os.unlink can mask the original error
findings.description: If os.replace succeeded but something later in the try block fails, or if the temp file no longer exists, os.unlink(tmp_name) raises FileNotFoundError. That exception replaces the original error, so the real cause (disk full, serialization error) is hidden. The bare except also catches BaseException, which is broader than needed.
findings.suggestion: Use `except BaseException:` with `try: os.unlink(tmp_name) except FileNotFoundError: pass` before re-raising, or use contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError).

findings.title: Expired sessions no longer removed on get
findings.description: The old get() deleted an expired session when it was looked up. The new get() only returns None, so expired sessions stay in memory (and in the file) until someone calls purge_expired. If nothing calls purge_expired, the store grows without bound, and FileSessionStore keeps writing expired entries to disk.
findings.suggestion: Make sure purge_expired is called periodically, or remove the expired entry under the write lock in get().

findings.title: Bare except with unguarded os.unlink can mask the original error
findings.description: If the failure happens after `os.replace` succeeded (not possible here), or if the temp file is already gone, `os.unlink(tmp_name)` raises FileNotFoundError inside the handler and replaces the original exception (e.g. disk full), hiding the real cause. The bare `except:` also intercepts KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit. The unlink failure also prevents `raise` from running.
findings.suggestion: Use `except BaseException:` with `try: os.unlink(tmp_name) except FileNotFoundError: pass` before `raise`, or `contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError)`.

findings.title: get() no longer evicts expired sessions
findings.description: The previous get() deleted an expired session when it was seen. Now expired sessions stay in memory (and in the persisted file) until purge_expired is called. If callers relied on get() for cleanup and never call purge_expired, the store grows without bound.
findings.suggestion: Ensure purge_expired is scheduled, or document that get() no longer evicts.

findings.title: Bare except with unguarded unlink can mask the original error
findings.description: If the failure happens after os.replace (or the temp file is already gone), os.unlink(tmp_name) raises FileNotFoundError inside the except block. That exception replaces the real write error and `raise` is never reached. The bare `except:` also catches KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit.
findings.suggestion: Use `except BaseException:` with `contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError)` around the unlink, or `except Exception:`, then re-raise the original error.

findings.title: Memory update after replace can diverge from disk
findings.description: super()._commit(sessions) runs after os.replace has already published the file. The in-memory assignment is trivial and unlikely to fail. But the unlink handler covers only the file operations, so any failure between the replace and the memory swap leaves disk and memory out of sync.
findings.suggestion: Keep the memory swap immediately adjacent to the replace and ensure no failure can occur between them.

findings.title: Oversized cursor digits raise an uncaught ValueError (500 instead of 400)
findings.description: The regex accepts any number of digits. On Python 3.11+, `int()` raises ValueError for strings over 4300 digits. That call sits outside the try block in `decode_cursor`, and `list_events` only catches `BadRequest`, so the ValueError propagates. A client can send a base64 cursor wrapping `v1:` plus about 4300 digits (roughly 5.8 KB of query string) and get a server error instead of a 400.
findings.suggestion: Bound the digit count in the regex (for example `[1-9][0-9]{0,18}`), or wrap the `int()` call and raise BadRequest on ValueError.

findings.title: SERVER_NAME parsing with partition(':') breaks IPv6 literals
findings.description: The previous code used urlsplit, which handled bracketed IPv6 addresses such as '[::1]:5000' and also lowercased the hostname. partition(':') splits at the first colon, so sn_host becomes '[' and sn_port becomes ':1]:5000'. The int(sn_port) call then raises ValueError, or the host is wrong, whenever app.run() is used with an IPv6 SERVER_NAME.
findings.suggestion: Keep urlsplit(f'//{server_name}') for parsing, or use rpartition(':') with bracket handling.

findings.title: Cookie domain lost 'localhost' fallback and breaks IPv6 hosts
findings.description: The old code used urlsplit(host_url).hostname or 'localhost'. The new code uses request.host.partition(':')[0]. For an IPv6 Host header like '[::1]:5000' this yields '[', which is the wrong cookie domain, so cookies saved by session_transaction are not matched on later requests. An empty host also yields '' instead of 'localhost'. Hostname case is also no longer normalised.
findings.suggestion: Restore urlsplit(ctx.request.host_url).hostname or 'localhost'.

findings.title: SERVER_NAME parsing with partition(":") breaks IPv6 literals
findings.description: The old code used urlsplit, which handled bracketed IPv6 hosts such as "[::1]:5000". With partition(":") that value becomes host "[" and port "":1]:5000"; int() then raises ValueError, or the host is wrong. SERVER_NAME values containing IPv6 addresses worked before and now break when app.run() is called.
findings.suggestion: Keep urlsplit(f"//{server_name}") for hostname and port parsing, or use rpartition(":") with bracket handling.

findings.title: Cookie domain from request.host breaks IPv6 hosts and drops the localhost fallback
findings.description: The old code took the hostname via urlsplit(host_url).hostname or "localhost". The new code uses host.partition(":")[0]. For an IPv6 host such as "[::1]:5000" this yields "[", so the session cookie gets stored under the wrong domain. If host is empty, the domain is an empty string instead of "localhost". Cookies saved by session_transaction then do not match later requests.
findings.suggestion: Restore urlsplit(ctx.request.host_url).hostname or "localhost".

findings.title: SERVER_NAME parsing with partition(":") breaks IPv6 literals
findings.description: The old code used urlsplit, which handled bracketed IPv6 hosts such as "[::1]:5000". partition(":") splits at the first colon, so sn_host becomes "[" and sn_port becomes ":1]:5000". app.run() then binds to host "[", and the later int(sn_port) raises ValueError. The old code also stripped brackets and lowercased the hostname, and that is lost too.
findings.suggestion: Keep using urlsplit(f"//{server_name}") for hostname and port, or use rpartition with bracket handling.

findings.title: Cookie domain no longer falls back to localhost and breaks on IPv6 hosts
findings.description: The old code used urlsplit(host_url).hostname or "localhost". The new code uses host.partition(":")[0]. For an IPv6 host such as "[::1]:5000" this yields "[", so the cookie domain is wrong and the session cookie is not sent on later requests. An empty host gives "" instead of "localhost". The hostname is also no longer lowercased.
findings.suggestion: Restore urlsplit(ctx.request.host_url).hostname or "localhost".

findings.title: RootModel.__copy__ now shares the private-attributes dict with the original
findings.description: The removed block rebuilt `__pydantic_private__` in the copied `__dict__`. On RootModel, private attribute values are kept in `__dict__['__pydantic_private__']`, because the class-level `__pydantic_private__ = None` shadows the slot. Without that block, `copy(self.__dict__)` is shallow, so the copy and the original reference the same private dict. Assigning a private attribute on one instance then silently changes the other. The filter for `PydanticUndefined` placeholders is also gone, so unset-private markers are carried into the copy.
findings.suggestion: Restore the copy of the private dict, with the `PydanticUndefined` filtering, when `__pydantic_private__` is present in `new_dict`.

findings.title: RootModel.__copy__ no longer copies private attributes
findings.description: RootModel sets `__pydantic_private__ = None` as a class attribute, which shadows the BaseModel slot, so a subclass's private attributes live in the instance `__dict__`. The removed block copied that private dict and dropped `PydanticUndefined` placeholders. `new_dict = copy(self.__dict__)` is only shallow, so after this change the copy and the original share the same private dict. Setting a private attribute on one therefore changes the other. Unset private attributes also stay as `PydanticUndefined` in the copy, so reading them returns the sentinel instead of raising AttributeError.
findings.suggestion: Restore the handling: after copying `__dict__`, replace `__pydantic_private__` with a new dict that omits `PydanticUndefined` values.

findings.title: UploadFile position no longer restored after reading bytes
findings.description: The removed `_read_file_bytes` helper saved the file position and seeked back after reading. The direct `value.read()` calls leave the file cursor at EOF. If the same UploadFile is read again (for example when the form is parsed a second time, or another dependency or field uses the same upload), it gets empty bytes. This is a regression from the previous behavior.
findings.suggestion: Restore `_read_file_bytes`, or otherwise save the position before `read()` and `await file.seek(position)` afterwards in both places.

findings.title: UploadFile position no longer restored after reading bytes
findings.description: The removed helper `_read_file_bytes` saved the file position and seeked back after reading. Now `value.read()` leaves the underlying file at EOF. If the same UploadFile is read again (for example when the body is parsed more than once, when another field or dependency also receives the same upload, or when `request.form()` is reused), it will return empty bytes. Data is silently lost on the second read, so the second consumer sees an empty upload.
findings.suggestion: Restore the position after reading: record `file.file.tell()` before the read and `await file.seek(position)` in a `finally` block, as the removed helper did. Alternatively, keep the helper and use it at both call sites.

findings.title: UploadFile position no longer restored after reading bytes
findings.description: The removed helper read the file and then seeked back to its original position. Now `value.read()` leaves the file pointer at EOF. The same UploadFile can be seen by another consumer, for example a parameter that declares the same form field as `UploadFile`, or a dependency that reads it again. That second reader gets empty content. The same applies if the field is validated or read twice, and the bytes path in the sequence branch has the same problem.
findings.suggestion: Restore the helper, or seek back to the original position after reading: `pos = value.file.tell(); data = await value.read(); await value.seek(pos)`.

findings.title: Awaiting the shared Deferred directly breaks multiple concurrent waiters
findings.description: The parser Deferred is shared by every request for the same netloc that arrives while robots.txt is being fetched. maybe_deferred_to_future(parser) adds a callback to that Deferred which returns None, or a plain value, and this callback sits in the chain ahead of later waiters. Whichever waiter attaches first consumes the result and leaves the Deferred's result as None, so the next waiter gets None. A None parser means process_request_2 skips the robots.txt check, so disallowed URLs are crawled. The removed code used a separate waiter Deferred per caller and returned the result through the chain, which avoided this. In asyncio mode the future adapter's callback also returns None.
findings.suggestion: Restore a per-caller waiter Deferred whose callback is chained on the shared Deferred and returns the result, so the chain value is preserved for the next waiter.

findings.title: Awaiting the shared Deferred directly breaks for multiple concurrent waiters
findings.description: The shared per-netloc Deferred is awaited directly by every request waiting on the same host's robots.txt. maybe_deferred_to_future adds a callback to the Deferred that returns None, so the result chain is consumed after the first waiter. Later waiters get None, and rp_dfd.callback(rp) hands the parser to the first waiter only. Other concurrent requests to that host then see rp=None in process_request_2 and skip the robots.txt check, so forbidden URLs are crawled. The removed per-waiter Deferred forwarded the result to each waiter without consuming the shared chain.
findings.suggestion: Restore a per-waiter Deferred that is fired from a callback on the shared Deferred, and return the result from that callback so the chain value is preserved.

findings.title: Multiple waiters share one Deferred, so later waiters get None or hang
findings.description: The removed code gave each waiter its own Deferred through a callback chained onto the shared one. Now every concurrent request for the same netloc awaits the same `parser` Deferred directly. `maybe_deferred_to_future` adds a callback that returns the result, but its result is not preserved for others. With the asyncio reactor it wraps the Deferred in a Future, and that Future's callback chain replaces the Deferred's result with None. With more than one waiter, or one waiter plus the request that created the parser, the later waiters see None, so robots.txt rules are silently skipped. Without asyncio, a `Deferred` returned to the awaiting coroutine can also raise AlreadyCalledError or give the wrong result. The first waiter can consume the result and the second get None, so forbidden URLs are crawled.
findings.suggestion: Restore a per-waiter Deferred that is fed from the shared one through a callback returning the result, as the removed code did, and await that one.

findings.title: Missing return after rejecting task with invalid ETA
findings.description: After `req.reject(requeue=False)` the handler no longer returns. `eta` stays None and execution falls through to the non-ETA path, which calls `task_reserved(req)`, the callbacks and `handle(req)`, so the already-rejected task is executed immediately. The message is rejected and may also be executed, and the ack/reject may happen twice. The task also runs without its ETA.
findings.suggestion: Restore the `return` after `req.reject(requeue=False)`.

findings.title: Task failure no longer recorded in result backend
findings.description: The removed `mark_as_failure` call stored the failure in the backend. Now the task is rejected without recording any result, so clients waiting on the result never see the failure and the task stays PENDING.
findings.suggestion: Restore the `req.task.backend.mark_as_failure(...)` call before rejecting.

findings.title: Missing return after rejecting task with invalid ETA
findings.description: The `return` after `req.reject(requeue=False)` was removed. When the ETA conversion fails, the request is rejected but execution continues: eta stays None, so the code reaches `task_reserved(req)` and `handle(req)` (or `limit_task` when a rate-limit bucket exists). A task that was just rejected and dropped is therefore also executed immediately, and it may be acked or rejected a second time.
findings.suggestion: Restore the `return` right after `req.reject(requeue=False)`.

findings.title: Failure no longer recorded in result backend
findings.description: The `mark_as_failure` call was removed, so a task with an unconvertible ETA is rejected without any failure state being stored. Clients waiting on the result never see a failure and may hang or see PENDING indefinitely.
findings.suggestion: Restore the `req.task.backend.mark_as_failure(...)` call before rejecting.

findings.title: Missing return after rejecting task with invalid ETA
findings.description: The `return` after `req.reject(requeue=False)` was removed. When the ETA cannot be converted, `eta` stays None and execution continues. The task is rejected (and acked/dropped) but then falls through to the rate-limit/bucket logic and is executed immediately via `task_reserved(req)` and `handle(req)`, or goes to `limit_task`. A task that was rejected as invalid therefore runs without its ETA, and is potentially processed after it was already rejected.
findings.suggestion: Restore the `return` after `req.reject(requeue=False)`.

findings.title: Failure no longer recorded in result backend for invalid ETA
findings.description: The call to `backend.mark_as_failure` was removed, so a task rejected because of an unparseable ETA leaves no failure state in the result backend. Clients waiting on the result will never see the failure and may hang or see PENDING indefinitely.
findings.suggestion: Restore the `mark_as_failure` call before rejecting the request.

findings.title: Cached result list returned by reference; callers can corrupt the cache
findings.description: Both the cache-hit path (line 63) and the miss path (line 68) return the same list object that is stored in the cache. If a caller sorts, appends to, or otherwise mutates the returned list, later find() calls with the same query and tags get the altered result until the TTL expires or the cache is cleared. Before this change every call returned a fresh list, so callers could mutate it safely.
findings.suggestion: Store a tuple internally and return list(...) copies, or return a copy on both the hit and miss paths, e.g. `return list(entry[1])` and `return list(hits)`.

findings.title: Cached result list returned by reference; callers can mutate the cache
findings.description: The same list object stored in the cache is returned on both the miss path (`return hits`) and the hit path (`return entry[1]`). Before this change each call returned a fresh list. A caller that sorts, appends to or filters the result in place now silently corrupts the cached entry, and later callers with the same query get the altered results.
findings.suggestion: Store a tuple in the cache and return `list(...)` copies, or return a copy on both paths.

findings.title: Cache hit refreshes LRU order but not the timestamp, and expired entries are handled inconsistently
findings.description: An expired entry is popped, so the cache shrinks, and then a recompute happens. The capacity check on line 65 therefore sees a length that already excludes that key, which is fine. However, the stored entry keeps its original timestamp when re-inserted on a hit, so the TTL is absolute from creation and the LRU ordering has no effect on expiry. This is only a minor inconsistency, not a hard failure.
findings.suggestion: Document the TTL semantics, or drop the LRU reordering if it is not needed.

findings.title: Cached result list is returned by reference and can be mutated by callers
findings.description: find() returns the exact list object stored in the cache, both on a hit (line 63) and on a miss (line 68). If a caller sorts, appends to or removes from the returned list, the cached entry is corrupted. Later callers with the same query get the altered results until the TTL expires or a product is added. Before this change each call returned a fresh list, so callers could mutate it safely.
findings.suggestion: Store a tuple internally and return list(entry[1]) on hits and list(hits) on misses, so callers never hold the cached list.

findings.title: deliver() coroutine is not awaited in flush()
findings.description: deliver is now async, but flush calls it without await. The call returns a coroutine object, which is always truthy, so every digest is treated as delivered. Nothing is ever sent, because the coroutine never runs (Python also emits a 'never awaited' warning). Pending lines are deleted, so digests are silently lost and `failed` is always empty.
findings.suggestion: Use `if await deliver(channel, message):`.

findings.title: Queue mutation across await can drop or corrupt lines
findings.description: flush now awaits during delivery, so add() can run in the meantime. The `sent` snapshot handles appends, but `self._pending[recipient]` is held as a local list. If another flush runs concurrently, or the key is deleted and re-created, the lines are removed twice or from a stale list. Concurrent flushes can also double-send digests. `sorted(self._pending)` is a snapshot, but `self._pending[recipient]` on a key deleted by another flush would create a new empty list and send an empty digest.
findings.suggestion: Guard flush with an asyncio.Lock, or snapshot the lines with `lines = list(self._pending[recipient])` and remove only the sent prefix afterwards, using `.get` to handle missing keys.

findings.title: Missing await on async deliver() makes every digest look delivered
findings.description: deliver is now a coroutine function, but flush calls it without await. The coroutine object is always truthy, so the branch is always taken and no message is ever sent (a 'coroutine was never awaited' warning is emitted). Lines are deleted from the queue as if delivered, so digests are silently lost and failed is always empty.
findings.suggestion: Use `if await deliver(channel, message):`.

findings.title: Iterating the pending dict across awaits while add() can mutate it
findings.description: Once the await is added, flush yields at each send, so add() can run concurrently. `sorted(self._pending)` takes a snapshot of the keys, so recipients added during the flush are skipped (fine). But `self._pending[recipient]` at line 42 raises KeyError if the key was removed meanwhile, for example by a concurrent flush. Two concurrent flushes can also both send the same lines and then double-delete via `del lines[:sent]`.
findings.suggestion: Guard flush with an asyncio.Lock and use `self._pending.get(recipient)`, skipping recipients that no longer exist.

findings.title: Missing await on async deliver() makes every digest look delivered
findings.description: deliver is now a coroutine function, but flush calls it without await. The coroutine object is always truthy, so the branch always takes the success path. No message is ever sent (the coroutine never runs, with a 'never awaited' warning), lines are deleted from the queue as if delivered, and failed is always empty. This is silent data loss of queued digests.
findings.suggestion: Use `if await deliver(channel, message):`.

findings.title: Mutating the list and deleting the dict key across an await can lose lines or raise
findings.description: Once deliver is awaited, other coroutines may call add() during the send. After the await, `del lines[:sent]` is correct only if the list object is still the same. The iteration `for recipient in sorted(self._pending)` uses a snapshot, so it is safe. But `del self._pending[recipient]` could race with a concurrent flush that already removed the key, raising KeyError. Also, render() is computed from all lines, which may exceed MAX_LINES, while only `sent` lines are removed, which is fine. The race on concurrent flushes is the issue.
findings.suggestion: Use `self._pending.pop(recipient, None)` and guard against concurrent flushes, for example with an asyncio.Lock.

findings.title: for_account filters on the removed `user_id` key
findings.description: `records()` now upgrades every record to the current schema, which drops `user_id` and sets `account_id`. `for_account` still compares `record.get("user_id")`, which is always None, so it never matches and yields nothing. `account_timeline` therefore always returns an empty list.
findings.suggestion: Compare `record.get("account_id") == account_id`.

findings.title: for_account filters on removed legacy key user_id
findings.description: records() now upgrades every record to the current schema, so `user_id` is removed and `account_id` is set. `record.get("user_id")` is therefore always None, and for_account never matches anything. account_timeline always returns an empty list.
findings.suggestion: Compare `record.get("account_id") == account_id`.

findings.title: for_account filters on removed legacy key user_id
findings.description: records() now returns records upgraded to the current schema, where `user_id` is removed and replaced by `account_id`. `record.get("user_id")` is therefore always None, so `for_account` never matches anything. `account_timeline` always returns an empty list.
findings.suggestion: Compare `record.get("account_id") == account_id`.

findings.title: decide() auto-approves reports that have policy violations
findings.description: `check()` used to return True when a report was within policy. It now returns a list of problems, which is empty when the report is within policy. `decide()` still does `if check(report, rates): APPROVED`, so a non-empty list (violations) is truthy and the report is approved. A compliant report has an empty list, which is falsy, so it is sent to NEEDS_REVIEW. The approval decision is inverted.
findings.suggestion: Use `if not check(report, rates): report.status = Status.APPROVED else: report.status = Status.NEEDS_REVIEW`.

findings.title: decide() treats the list of problems as a pass/fail boolean, inverting the result
findings.description: `check` now returns a list of violation messages, empty when the report is within policy. `decide` still does `if check(report, rates):`, and a non-empty list is truthy. Reports with violations (over the limit, or missing a receipt) are now auto-approved. Clean reports return an empty list, which is falsy, so they are sent to NEEDS_REVIEW. This bypasses the spending policy.
findings.suggestion: Invert the condition: `if not check(report, rates): report.status = Status.APPROVED else: report.status = Status.NEEDS_REVIEW`.

findings.title: decide() treats the non-empty problem list as "within policy", inverting approval
findings.description: check() now returns a list of violation messages that is empty when the report is within policy. decide() still uses `if check(report, rates):`, which is true when there are violations. Reports that break policy are auto-approved, and clean reports are sent to NEEDS_REVIEW.
findings.suggestion: Approve only when the list is empty: `if not check(report, rates): report.status = Status.APPROVED else: report.status = Status.NEEDS_REVIEW`.

findings.title: create_ticket still passes renamed `attempts=1` kwarg, so non-idempotent POST is retried and body is polluted
findings.description: The client parameter was renamed from `attempts` to `max_attempts`, but create_ticket still passes `attempts=1`. It is no longer recognised, so it falls into `**fields` and is sent as a JSON body field `attempts`. `max_attempts` stays at the default of 3. A transport timeout or 5xx on this non-idempotent POST is now retried up to 3 times with backoff, which can create duplicate tickets. The vendor API may also reject the unknown `attempts` field.
findings.suggestion: Change `attempts=1` to `max_attempts=1` in the create_ticket call.

findings.title: create_ticket still passes the renamed `attempts` kwarg, so it becomes a JSON body field
findings.description: `HelpdeskClient.request` renamed its `attempts` parameter to `max_attempts`. This call site was not updated, so `attempts=1` now falls into `**fields` and is sent as `{"attempts": 1}` in the ticket body. The non-idempotent POST also loses its single-attempt protection and uses the default of 3 attempts. A timeout or 5xx will retry and can create duplicate tickets. The vendor API may also reject the unknown field.
findings.suggestion: Change `attempts=1` to `max_attempts=1`. Also grep for any other callers still using `attempts=`.

findings.title: create_ticket still passes renamed `attempts` kwarg, so retries are not disabled
findings.description: `HelpdeskClient.request` renamed its `attempts` parameter to `max_attempts`. `create_ticket` still passes `attempts=1`, which now falls into `**fields` and is sent as a JSON body field. The non-idempotent POST is therefore retried up to 3 times, with backoff, on transport errors or 5xx, which can create duplicate tickets. The vendor API also receives an unexpected `attempts` field in the body, which may be rejected or ignored.
findings.suggestion: Change `attempts=1` to `max_attempts=1` in the `create_ticket` call.

findings.title: Sink write failures are caught and recorded as a rejected row
findings.description: The try block wraps self._flush, so any exception from sink.write (I/O error, DB outage) is caught by `except Exception`. The whole batch has been detached from `batch` (line 65), so up to batch_size rows are silently dropped, yet only the single current row is recorded as rejected, with the sink error as its reason. The load continues and returns a report that looks mostly successful, though rows were lost. Sink errors are not row-level parse errors and should propagate.
findings.suggestion: Only wrap parse_row in the try/except; call self._flush outside it so sink failures propagate (or are handled separately).

findings.title: Over-broad except Exception hides non-parse bugs
findings.description: Catching Exception around parsing turns programming errors (e.g. AttributeError, TypeError from a bug in parse_row) into per-row rejections, up to max_rejected. Only the expected parse/validation errors should be treated as malformed rows.
findings.suggestion: Catch the specific exception(s) parse_row raises, e.g. ValueError or a ParseError class.

findings.title: Sink write failures are caught and recorded as a row rejection
findings.description: The try block wraps self._flush(), so any exception from sink.write (I/O error, DB outage) is caught by `except Exception`. The whole batch is lost, because `batch` was already reset to [] before the flush. A single failed row number is recorded as rejected for what was really a batch-wide write failure. The loop keeps going, so a dead sink silently drops data. The report's loaded count does not include these rows and no error propagates, apart from TooManyRejected much later.
findings.suggestion: Only wrap parse_row in the try/except. Call self._flush outside it, so sink errors propagate. Catch specific parse exceptions (e.g. ValueError, KeyError) rather than Exception.

findings.title: Sink write failures are caught and recorded as a single bad row rejection
findings.description: The try block wraps `self._flush(...)` as well as `parse_row`. If `sink.write` raises (DB outage, IO error), the exception is swallowed and the current row is recorded as rejected with the sink's error message. The batch was already reset to [], so up to batch_size rows are silently dropped and never loaded, and none of them are reported as rejected except the one row. The load continues and returns a report that looks mostly clean. Sink errors should propagate, or at least not be treated as row-level parse errors.
findings.suggestion: Limit the try/except to `parse_row` only (catch the specific parse error such as ValueError), and call `_flush` outside the try so sink failures propagate.

findings.title: Over-broad `except Exception` hides programming errors as row rejections
findings.description: Catching every Exception around parse_row treats bugs such as TypeError, KeyError from code defects, or MemoryError-like failures as bad data. Systematic bugs cause every row to be rejected up to max_rejected, producing misleading reasons.
findings.suggestion: Catch only the parse/validation exceptions that parse_row is documented to raise.

findings.title: RetryingGateway.charge returns None after retries are exhausted instead of raising
findings.description: When the last attempt fails, the loop hits `break` and the function ends without a return or raise, so `charge` returns None. `settle_invoice` only catches GatewayError, so it then runs `charge.id` on None and raises AttributeError. Any persistent gateway failure now crashes the whole settlement batch, and the invoice is never marked PAYMENT_FAILED. Before this change the GatewayError was caught and recorded.
findings.suggestion: Re-raise the last GatewayError once attempts are exhausted (`raise` instead of `break`), or keep the exception and raise it after the loop.

findings.title: All GatewayErrors are retried, including non-transient ones
findings.description: Every GatewayError triggers a retry with backoff, including permanent failures such as a card decline or invalid customer. Each such invoice then sleeps through the full backoff (0.5s + 1s by default) before failing, which slows the batch and repeats calls that cannot succeed.
findings.suggestion: Retry only errors marked transient (for example a `retryable` attribute or a subclass), and re-raise the others immediately.

findings.title: charge() returns None after exhausting retries instead of raising
findings.description: When the final attempt fails, the loop hits `break` and the method falls off the end, returning None. settle_invoice only catches GatewayError, so it takes the success path: it sets the invoice to PAID and reads `charge.id` on None, raising AttributeError. The failed-charge handling (PAYMENT_FAILED) is never reached, and the AttributeError aborts the whole settle_open_invoices batch, leaving the remaining invoices unsettled.
findings.suggestion: Re-raise the last GatewayError after the final attempt (replace `break` with `raise`), or raise a new GatewayError after the loop.

findings.title: charge() returns None after retries are exhausted instead of raising
findings.description: When the final attempt fails, the loop breaks and the function falls off the end, returning None instead of a Charge or raising. In settle_invoice, `except GatewayError` is never triggered for exhausted retries, so execution continues to `charge.id` and raises AttributeError on None. That aborts the whole settle_open_invoices run, and the invoice is never marked PAYMENT_FAILED.
findings.suggestion: Keep the last exception and re-raise it after the loop (e.g. `raise` in place of `break`, or `raise last_exc`).

findings.title: finally block overwrites the retry-delay next_run on every run
findings.description: The `finally` clause sets `job.next_run = now + job.interval` after both the success and failure paths. On failure it overwrites the `now + self._retry_delay(job)` set at line 65, so the backoff is computed and then discarded. Failed jobs are retried only after the full interval, and `retry_delay` has no effect.
findings.suggestion: Set `job.next_run = now + job.interval` only in the `else` branch (success), or remove the `finally` block and keep the failure-path assignment.

findings.title: finally block overwrites the retry-backed-off next_run
findings.description: The `finally` clause always runs after the except block and sets `job.next_run = now + job.interval`. This overwrites the `now + self._retry_delay(job)` set at line 65 on failure. Failed jobs are therefore never retried sooner, so the new retry_delay/backoff feature has no effect.
findings.suggestion: Set `job.next_run = now + job.interval` only in the `else` branch, or remove the `finally` and keep the assignment in each branch.

findings.title: finally block overwrites the backoff next_run on failure
findings.description: The `finally` clause always runs after the except branch, so `job.next_run = now + job.interval` overwrites the `now + self._retry_delay(job)` set at line 65. Failed jobs are therefore never retried sooner, and the retry_delay feature has no effect. Only the success path should schedule at `interval`.
findings.suggestion: Remove the `finally` and set `job.next_run = now + job.interval` in the `else` branch only.

findings.title: Unbounded exponent in backoff computation can overflow
findings.description: `job.retry_delay * 2 ** (consecutive_failures - 1)` grows without bound. If `max_failures` is large, or failures keep accumulating, the multiplication eventually raises OverflowError (timedelta overflow) inside the except handler. That exception escapes `_run` and `tick`, so the remaining due jobs are skipped and no record is appended.
findings.suggestion: Cap the exponent, e.g. `2 ** min(job.consecutive_failures - 1, 20)`, or double iteratively and stop once the value reaches `interval`.

findings.title: Read failures are treated as an empty store, so sessions get wiped
findings.description: _read_all returns {} on OSError, ValueError or KeyError, including a corrupt or temporarily unreadable file. The next save, delete or take_by_refresh then rewrites the file from that empty dict, which silently drops every other live session. Sessions that should still be revoked are lost, and users are logged out. The same masking means sign_out_everywhere and purge_expired see no records during a read failure and report success. A missing file is the only case that should map to empty.
findings.suggestion: Return {} only for FileNotFoundError. Raise StoreError for other OSError and for parse errors, so writers do not overwrite the file with an empty or partial state.

findings.title: Refresh token is consumed before validation and the user lookup is not guarded
findings.description: take_by_refresh deletes the session before the user check and before _issue. If _issue's save fails with a StoreError, the old session is already gone and no new one exists, so the user is logged out. The same happens when a transient failure occurs between take and save.
findings.suggestion: Handle the failure of _issue after take, for example by restoring the old record on error, or make the rotation a single atomic store operation.

findings.title: purge_expired does not tolerate StoreError, unlike sign_out_everywhere
findings.description: A StoreError on one delete aborts the loop partway. The remaining expired records are not purged and the caller gets an exception instead of a count. The returned count is also len(expired), not the number actually deleted.
findings.suggestion: Catch StoreError per record as in sign_out_everywhere and count only successful deletes.

findings.title: Failed revocation is swallowed in sign_out_everywhere and change_password
findings.description: When delete raises StoreError, it is only logged and the session stays valid. change_password still returns normally, so the caller believes all sessions ended after a password change even though some tokens, including the refresh token, still work. Only a count is returned, with no indication of failure.
findings.suggestion: After the loop, raise if any revocation failed, or return or raise a failure indicator so change_password cannot report success while sessions remain.

findings.title: Unlocked reads race with the writer
findings.description: FileSessionStore.get and all read without taking the lock. The memory store also reads without a lock in get. This is combined with the read-modify-write sequences under the lock. Reads are atomic with respect to os.replace, but all() followed by delete in sign_out_everywhere can miss a session saved concurrently, for example a login racing a password change.
findings.suggestion: Take the lock in the read methods. For revocation, make the per-user delete a single atomic store operation.

findings.title: Read errors treated as an empty store, causing silent session loss
findings.description: _read_all returns {} on OSError, ValueError or KeyError. A corrupt or transiently unreadable file looks like an empty store. The next save/delete/take_by_refresh then writes back only the new record, wiping every other live session. Also, TypeError/AttributeError from malformed items are not caught. Separately, sign_out_everywhere reads an empty list on a read failure and reports 0 revoked while sessions remain, so a password change would silently leave sessions alive.
findings.suggestion: Return {} only for FileNotFoundError. Raise StoreError for other read or parse failures so callers and writers do not overwrite or ignore the existing data.

findings.title: File store get/all read without the lock
findings.description: FileSessionStore.get and all call _read_all without taking self._lock, while writers rewrite the file under the lock. os.replace is atomic so reads usually see a whole file. But the shared '.tmp' file and the read-modify-write sequences are only protected among writers in one process. Readers can return stale data to sign_out_everywhere, which then misses a session saved concurrently, e.g. a login racing a password change.
findings.suggestion: Take the lock in get and all, or document and handle the stale snapshot in callers.

findings.title: Refresh token consumed before validity checks, and new session issue can fail after consumption
findings.description: refresh() removes the old session via take_by_refresh before checking the user is active. If _issue then fails with a StoreError, the old session is already destroyed and no new one exists, so the user is logged out. This is a partial failure that leaves bad state.
findings.suggestion: Handle the failure of the issue step, e.g. by restoring the taken record on error, or by issuing the new session before deleting the old one within one atomic store operation.

findings.title: purge_expired aborts on the first store error
findings.description: Unlike sign_out_everywhere, purge_expired does not catch StoreError around delete. One failed delete raises out of the loop, leaving the remaining expired sessions unpurged and losing the count. The returned count also claims all were deleted.
findings.suggestion: Catch StoreError per record, log it, and count only successful deletions.

findings.title: sign_out_everywhere can miss concurrently created sessions and leaves refresh race
findings.description: sign_out_everywhere takes a snapshot of all records and deletes by access hash. A refresh in flight can take_by_refresh a record (removing it from the store, so the snapshot delete is a no-op) and then _issue a new session after the password change. The refresh only checked active, not that the password changed. The attacker's refresh token therefore survives a password change.
findings.suggestion: Add a store-level delete_by_user operation that is atomic, and invalidate refresh in-flight, e.g. via a per-user session generation checked in _issue.

findings.title: sign_out_everywhere swallows StoreError, so change_password can leave live sessions
findings.description: When deleting a session fails with StoreError, the error is logged and skipped, and the method returns a count that merely excludes the failure. change_password calls this right after the password changed, so a failed revoke leaves an old session valid, and the caller cannot tell. Sessions that should have been revoked after a password change stay usable.
findings.suggestion: Collect failures and raise a StoreError after trying all of them, or return/raise so the caller knows revocation was incomplete.

findings.title: _read_all treats a corrupt or unreadable file as an empty store, and the next write wipes all sessions
findings.description: Any OSError, ValueError or KeyError makes _read_all return {}. save, delete and take_by_refresh then read-modify-write on that empty dict, so one transient read error or malformed file causes every other session to be silently erased. get/all also report no sessions, which logs everyone out and makes sign_out_everywhere revoke nothing without any error being raised.
findings.suggestion: Return {} only for FileNotFoundError; raise StoreError for other read or parse errors.

findings.title: Unlocked reads race with writes, and readers share the temp file
findings.description: FileSessionStore.get and all read without the lock. Reads use os.replace atomically, so partial files are unlikely, but combined with _read_all swallowing errors any failed read returns an empty result (a valid session appears invalid). MemorySessionStore.get also reads the dict without the lock.
findings.suggestion: Take the lock in get/all, or make _read_all raise on errors.

findings.title: purge_expired aborts midway on a StoreError and its count is unreliable
findings.description: Unlike sign_out_everywhere, purge_expired does not handle StoreError: one failed delete aborts the purge halfway. It also returns len(expired) regardless of how many deletes actually removed something, which includes sessions already removed concurrently. This is also inconsistent with the other method's handling.
findings.suggestion: Handle StoreError per record and count only successful deletes.

findings.title: Refresh consumes the old session before validation and issuing, so a failure loses the session
findings.description: take_by_refresh deletes the record atomically. If the user lookup raises or _issue's save fails with StoreError, the old session is already destroyed and no new one is issued, so the client is logged out by a transient failure.
findings.suggestion: Issue the new session first, or restore the old record when a later step fails.

findings.title: Conditional expression precedence zeroes the score of every term not in the title
findings.description: `frequency + title_bonus if term in title_terms else 0.0` parses as `(frequency + title_bonus) if term in title_terms else 0.0`. Every term absent from the title gets a score of 0.0 instead of its frequency. With the default empty title, all scores are 0.0 and the ranking falls back to alphabetical order. In suggest_tags, every keyword then fails `score >= MIN_SCORE`, so no tags are suggested for articles whose title shares no terms with the body. The existing extract_keywords behavior of ranking by frequency is broken.
findings.suggestion: Write `scores[term] = frequency + (title_bonus if term in title_terms else 0.0)`.

findings.title: Conditional expression precedence zeroes score of every non-title term
findings.description: `scores[term] = frequency + title_bonus if term in title_terms else 0.0` parses as `(frequency + title_bonus) if term in title_terms else 0.0`. Every term not in the title gets a score of 0.0 instead of its frequency. With no title (the default), all scores are 0, so extract_keywords returns alphabetically-sorted terms with score 0.0. In suggest_tags, nothing then passes MIN_SCORE, so no tags are suggested for articles without title overlap.
findings.suggestion: Write `scores[term] = frequency + (title_bonus if term in title_terms else 0.0)`.

findings.title: Conditional expression precedence zeroes the score of every term not in the title
findings.description: `frequency + title_bonus if term in title_terms else 0.0` parses as `(frequency + title_bonus) if term in title_terms else 0.0`. Every term absent from the title gets a score of 0.0 instead of its frequency. With the default empty title, all scores are 0.0 and the ranking falls back to alphabetical order. suggest_tags then filters on `score >= MIN_SCORE`, so it returns no suggestions for most articles. The scores that are returned are also wrong.
findings.suggestion: Write `scores[term] = frequency + (title_bonus if term in title_terms else 0.0)`.

findings.title: Refill is double-counted after a denied request because updated_at is not advanced
findings.description: On a denied check, `bucket.tokens` is already increased by the elapsed refill, but `bucket.updated_at` is left at its old value. The next call computes `elapsed` from that same old timestamp and adds the refill again. Example: capacity 10, rate 1/s, tokens 0 at t=0. A cost-5 request at t=3 is denied and tokens become 3. At t=4 the elapsed time is 4 s, giving 7 tokens instead of the correct 4, so the request is allowed. Clients that keep retrying while limited get far more throughput than the configured rate, and the Retry-After values are too short.
findings.suggestion: Set `bucket.updated_at = now` right after applying the refill, before the `bucket.tokens < cost` check, so it is updated on both the allow and deny paths.

findings.title: Burst smaller than request cost makes expensive requests permanently denied
findings.description: The `burst` config can be set below 5, the cost of expensive paths. The bucket can then never hold enough tokens, so `/v1/search` and `/v1/export` always return 429. The Retry-After value computed in that case is meaningless, because the wait never ends. Nothing validates this at build time.
findings.suggestion: Validate that burst is at least the maximum request cost, or cap the cost at capacity.

findings.title: Denied requests double-count token refill
findings.description: On refill, `bucket.tokens` is increased, but `bucket.updated_at` is only advanced on the allowed path. When a request is denied (line 71 returns early), the refilled tokens are kept while `updated_at` stays old. The next call computes `elapsed` from the old timestamp and adds the same interval's refill again. Example: capacity 10, rate 1/s, tokens 0 at t=0. A cost-10 request denied at t=5 leaves tokens=5 and updated_at=0. At t=6 elapsed=6, so tokens become 11 and are capped to 10, when only 6 should be available. Clients that keep retrying while limited therefore get more throughput than the configured rate.
findings.suggestion: Set `bucket.updated_at = now` immediately after the refill on line 69, before the `bucket.tokens < cost` check, so it advances on both the allowed and denied paths.

findings.title: Token refill is double-counted after a denied request
findings.description: check() adds the refill to bucket.tokens on every call, but updated_at is only advanced on the allowed path. When a request is denied, the refilled tokens are kept and updated_at stays old. The next call computes elapsed from that old timestamp and adds the same interval's refill again. Example: capacity 10, rate 1/s, empty bucket at t=0. A denied call at t=5 leaves tokens=5. At t=6 the bucket should hold 6 tokens, but it computes 5+6 and caps at 10. Clients that keep retrying while limited therefore get a full bucket back far sooner than the configured rate, so the limit is exceeded.
findings.suggestion: Set bucket.updated_at = now right after applying the refill (line 69), before the allow/deny decision, so each interval is credited only once.

findings.title: Previous-month lookup uses wrong key order
findings.description: UsageKey is (account_id, metric, month), but the lookup builds (account_id, prior, metric). It never matches, so previous_total is always None and every change shows n/a. The month-over-month feature does not work.
findings.suggestion: Use usage.get((account_id, metric, prior)).

findings.title: Daily quantity accumulator is not reset between groups
findings.description: After yielding a DailyTotal when the key changes, quantity is not reset to 0. The next group starts with the previous group's total added in, so every day after the first is inflated by cumulative sums. All totals, peaks and averages are wrong.
findings.suggestion: Set quantity = 0 after the yield, before adding the current event's quantity.

findings.title: Zero previous total conflated with missing
findings.description: `not self.previous_total` treats 0 the same as None. That is acceptable for avoiding division by zero, but the previous_total column shows 0 while change shows n/a; this is inconsistent but minor.
findings.suggestion: Handle None and 0 explicitly if different output is wanted.

findings.title: Previous-month lookup uses wrong key order
findings.description: UsageKey is (account_id, metric, month), but the lookup builds (account_id, prior, metric). It never matches, so previous_total is always None and every change shows n/a.
findings.suggestion: Use usage.get((account_id, metric, prior)).

findings.title: Daily quantity accumulator is never reset between groups
findings.description: After yielding a DailyTotal when the key changes, `quantity` is not reset to 0. Each following day, metric or account inherits the previous group's quantity, so all totals, peaks and averages are inflated.
findings.suggestion: Reset `quantity = 0` after the yield, before adding the current event's quantity.

findings.title: Previous-month lookup uses wrong key order
findings.description: UsageKey is (account_id, metric, month), but the lookup uses (account_id, prior, metric). It never matches, so previous_total is always None and change is always 'n/a'. The month-over-month feature never works.
findings.suggestion: Use usage.get((account_id, metric, prior)).

findings.title: Quantity accumulator not reset between groups
findings.description: After yielding a DailyTotal when the key changes, `quantity` is not reset to 0. The next day/metric/account starts with the previous group's total added to it, so all daily totals after the first are inflated, as are monthly totals, peaks and averages.
findings.suggestion: Set quantity = 0 after the yield, before adding the current event's quantity.

findings.title: Zero previous total hidden while previous_total is shown
findings.description: `if not self.previous_total` treats a previous total of 0 as nothing to compare. This is arguably intended to avoid division by zero, but the guard also hides legitimate cases; it is minor.
findings.suggestion: Keep the zero guard but make the intent explicit (`is None or == 0`).

findings.title: Mutable default argument is mutated by setdefault
findings.description: `metadata` defaults to a shared `{}`, and `put` calls `metadata.setdefault("content-type", ...)` on it. The first call without metadata stores a guessed content type (e.g. text/csv) in the shared default dict. Every later put without metadata then keeps that stale type, so a .png uploaded after a .csv is labelled text/csv. Callers' own dicts are also mutated.
findings.suggestion: Use `metadata: dict[str, str] | None = None` and build a fresh copy: `metadata = dict(metadata or {})` before calling setdefault.

findings.title: Metadata written before blob, leaving inconsistent state on failure
findings.description: The metadata file is replaced before the blob is written. If the blob write fails (disk full, crash), the old blob stays paired with the new metadata, and for a new key an orphan meta file is left. Concurrent puts to the same key can also mix one writer's metadata with another's data. The temp file names are fixed and shared, so concurrent writers can also clobber each other.
findings.suggestion: Write the blob first, then the metadata. Clean up temp files on failure and use unique temp names.

findings.title: head can raise on corrupt metadata or when the file is deleted concurrently
findings.description: The `is_file()` check followed by `read_text` is a race: if a concurrent delete removes the meta file in between, FileNotFoundError escapes. Corrupt JSON raises JSONDecodeError out of head(). A non-dict JSON value would make `pop` fail.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the read and parse in try/except (FileNotFoundError, ValueError) and fall back to {}.

findings.title: Key-validation gap: user key can collide with metadata files
findings.description: Key parts may not start with '.', so hidden meta files are not reachable as keys, which is fine. But a key such as `a.meta.json` is valid while its metadata sidecar is `.a.meta.json`, and the sidecar of key `x` can never conflict. There is an ordering issue instead: the key `a` and a key `a/b` collide as file vs directory. This is not new, though, so it is a minor concern.

findings.title: Mutable default argument is mutated by setdefault
findings.description: `metadata` defaults to a shared `{}` and `put` calls `metadata.setdefault("content-type", ...)` on it. The first put without metadata stores a guessed content type in the shared default dict, and every later put without metadata reuses that type, so e.g. a .png after a .txt is stored as text/plain. A caller-supplied dict is also mutated.
findings.suggestion: Use `metadata: dict[str,str] | None = None`, then `metadata = dict(metadata or {})` before setdefault.

findings.title: Metadata written before blob; failure or key collision leaves inconsistent state
findings.description: The metadata file is replaced before the blob is written. If writing the blob fails, the old blob stays with the new metadata (wrong content type/user metadata). Overwrites are also non-atomic as a pair, and a concurrent head() can see mismatched data.
findings.suggestion: Write the blob first, then the metadata, or clean up and restore on failure.

findings.title: Corrupt or non-dict metadata file crashes head()
findings.description: `json.loads` on a truncated or invalid meta file raises JSONDecodeError, which is not handled. If the JSON is not an object, `.pop` fails with AttributeError. A missing-meta race between is_file and read_text can also raise FileNotFoundError.
findings.suggestion: Catch (OSError, ValueError) and fall back to {}, and verify the result is a dict.

findings.title: Mutable default argument is mutated by setdefault
findings.description: `metadata` defaults to a shared dict `{}`, and `put` calls `metadata.setdefault("content-type", ...)` on it. The first put without metadata stores a guessed content type in the shared default, so every later put without metadata reuses that type, e.g. a .png then a .pdf gets image/png. A caller-supplied dict is also mutated.
findings.suggestion: Use `metadata: dict[str, str] | None = None` and build a copy: `meta = dict(metadata or {}); meta.setdefault(...)`.

findings.title: Metadata written before blob; failed blob write leaves inconsistent state
findings.description: The metadata file is replaced before the blob is written. If the blob write fails, or a concurrent reader calls head in between, the old blob is paired with the new metadata. A new key whose blob write failed leaves an orphaned metadata file. The two atomic replaces are not atomic together.
findings.suggestion: Write the blob first, then the metadata, or clean up the metadata on failure.

findings.title: head can fail on a missing or corrupt metadata file
findings.description: `is_file()` followed by `read_text` is a check-then-act race with a concurrent delete, which raises FileNotFoundError. Corrupt JSON raises JSONDecodeError. Both escape instead of falling back to defaults.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the read and parse in try/except (FileNotFoundError, ValueError) and fall back to {}.

findings.title: Membership test against a list inside the scan loop is quadratic
findings.description: `active_skus` is built as a list, and `scan.sku not in active_skus` does a linear scan for every scan. With a large catalog and many scans (a typical stocktake), this costs O(scans × skus) and can make reconcile very slow.
findings.suggestion: Build `active_skus` as a set: `{item.sku for item in catalog.active()}`.

findings.title: Linear list membership test inside scan loop gives quadratic work
findings.description: active_skus is a list, so `scan.sku not in active_skus` scans the whole list for every scan. With a large catalog and many scans (the usual stocktake case), this costs O(scans × skus) instead of O(scans + skus).
findings.suggestion: Build a set: `active_skus = {item.sku for item in catalog.active()}`.

findings.title: Linear list membership test inside scan loop makes unknown_locations quadratic
findings.description: active_skus is a list, so `scan.sku not in active_skus` scans the whole list for every scan. With a large catalog and many scans (a stocktake can have hundreds of thousands) this is O(scans × skus) and will be very slow.
findings.suggestion: Build a set: `active_skus = {item.sku for item in catalog.active()}`.

findings.title: Per-year holiday cache removed; source is queried on every is_business_day call
findings.description: The `_holidays_by_year` cache was dropped, so `holidays()` now calls `self._source.holidays(...)` and builds a new frozenset each time. `is_business_day` calls it for every candidate day, and `add_business_days`, `business_days_between` and `roll_forward` step one day at a time. With `JsonHolidaySource`, every step re-reads and re-parses the whole JSON file from disk. `SlaPolicy.overdue` repeats this for every ticket, and each ticket calls `is_business_day` several times. The cost grows with tickets times days times file size.
findings.suggestion: Cache holidays per year inside `BusinessCalendar`, as before, keyed by year since the region is fixed per instance. Alternatively, cache in the source.

findings.title: Per-year holiday cache removed, so the holiday file is re-read and re-parsed on every day check
findings.description: `holidays()` used to memoize per year. It now calls `self._source.holidays(...)` every time. `JsonHolidaySource.holidays` reads and parses the whole JSON file on each call. `is_business_day` calls `holidays()` once per day, so `add_business_days`, `business_days_between`, `roll_forward` and `SlaPolicy.overdue` do a disk read and JSON parse per day stepped. With `overdue` over many tickets, that means thousands of file reads.
findings.suggestion: Restore a per-year cache inside `BusinessCalendar` (keyed by year, since the calendar is already per region), or cache the parsed JSON in `JsonHolidaySource`.

findings.title: Per-year holiday cache removed; source is queried on every is_business_day call
findings.description: holidays() used to memoize per year. It now calls self._source.holidays(...) every time. JsonHolidaySource re-reads and re-parses the whole JSON file on each call. is_business_day runs once per day in add_business_days, roll_forward and business_days_between, and SlaPolicy calls these for every ticket. A single due-date calculation therefore does many file reads and JSON parses, and overdue() over many tickets multiplies that.
findings.suggestion: Restore a per-year cache inside BusinessCalendar, for example a dict keyed by year. CalendarSet already holds one calendar per region, so the cache stays per region.

findings.title: Render failure aborts the whole campaign mid-send
findings.description: render() is called outside the try block. A subscriber-specific failure there, such as a body template containing other braces that raise KeyError/IndexError/ValueError in str.format, aborts send_campaign partway. Earlier recipients have already been emailed and the report is lost, so a retry would re-send to them.
findings.suggestion: Handle render errors per subscriber, record them in the report, and continue. Validate the template before sending starts.

findings.title: Render failure aborts the whole campaign mid-send
findings.description: render() runs outside the try block. If a subscriber's rendering raises (for example body_template.format hits a KeyError/IndexError/ValueError on a stray brace, or a bad address in Message), the exception propagates out of send_campaign. The loop stops, the report with already-sent recipients is lost, and the caller cannot tell who received the email. Re-running the campaign would then resend to those who already got it.
findings.suggestion: Move render() inside error handling, record per-subscriber failures in the report, and continue. Also handle other mailer errors, so that one bad recipient does not abort the batch and discard the report.

findings.title: Render failure aborts the whole campaign mid-send
findings.description: render() is called outside the try block. campaign.body_template.format(first_name=...) can raise KeyError, IndexError or ValueError if the template contains other braces or placeholders. The exception propagates out of send_campaign, so the loop stops partway and the caller never receives the CampaignReport. Subscribers already emailed are lost from the report, and a retry would send to them again.
findings.suggestion: Move render() inside the try block and handle or record render errors per subscriber. Alternatively, validate the template before the loop.

findings.title: Calibration loaded from the database once per reading instead of once per sensor
findings.description: The old code loaded each sensor's calibration once per batch, with a dict keyed by sensor_id. The new `calibrated()` calls `source.load()` for every reading, and `SqlCalibrationSource.load` runs a SQL query each time. A batch of N readings from a few sensors now issues N queries instead of one per distinct sensor. A sensor whose calibration changes mid-batch could also be calibrated inconsistently.
findings.suggestion: Cache calibrations per sensor_id within `summarize`, for example with a local dict, and pass the loaded calibration into the per-reading calibration step.

findings.title: Misleading reason when a zone is inspected because of a low rejected share check
findings.description: The inspect reason always reads "N readings out of range". It does not say whether the zone was flagged because every reading was rejected or because the rejected share exceeded the threshold. For a zone with `mean is None`, the count of rejected readings is the whole story, but the message does not explain why inspection was triggered.
findings.suggestion: Include the rejected share or total count in the reason, e.g. f"{rejected} of {total} readings out of range".

findings.title: Calibration loaded from the database for every reading
findings.description: The old code built a per-sensor calibration dict, so `source.load` ran once per distinct sensor. The new code calls `calibrated()` for each reading, and that calls `source.load`, which runs the SQL query. A batch with N readings now makes N queries instead of one per sensor, which is an N+1 pattern on a large batch.
findings.suggestion: Cache calibrations per sensor_id within `summarize`, for example with a local dict, and pass the cached Calibration to the range check.

findings.title: Calibration loaded from the database for every reading
findings.description: The old code loaded each distinct sensor's calibration once per batch. The new `calibrated()` calls `source.load()` for every reading, so a batch with N readings runs N SQL queries instead of one per sensor. Large batches become slow and put needless load on the database.
findings.suggestion: Cache calibrations per sensor_id within `summarize` (a dict, or a local memo passed into `calibrated`) so each sensor is loaded once per batch.

findings.title: Inspect reason is misleading when there are no rejected readings
findings.description: A zone is marked 'inspect' when `mean is None` or the rejected share is too high. The reason always says '{rejected} readings out of range'. With a policy where `max_rejected_share` is below the actual share the message is accurate, but a zone with `mean is None` and `rejected == 0` cannot occur from `summarize`. For other callers building summaries by hand, the message would read '0 readings out of range', which hides the real cause.
findings.suggestion: Build the reason from the actual condition, for example 'no valid readings' versus 'X of Y readings rejected'.

findings.title: Invalid marker keyed only by impression id, not campaign
findings.description: The invalid record stores only the impression id. `for_day` filters campaign records, but `invalid` is built from all records regardless of campaign, which is fine only if ids are globally unique. More importantly, the marker is written to the file of `served_at.date()`, and `for_day` reads only that day's file, so this works only when the same impression object is passed. If the id is reused across campaigns, a refund voids both campaigns' impressions.
findings.suggestion: Include campaign_id in the invalid record and match on (campaign, id).

findings.title: Whole day file re-read and parsed on every bid check
findings.description: `can_bid` calls `spend`, which calls `for_day`. That reads and JSON-parses the whole day file for every campaign on every bid request, replacing the previous O(1) in-memory counters. `eligible` multiplies this by the number of campaigns, so cost grows with the day's impression count on the hot bidding path.
findings.suggestion: Keep cached per-campaign/day hourly totals, updated on record and refund, or index the log.

findings.title: Hourly bucketing ignores timezone consistency with request time
findings.description: Spend is bucketed by `impression.served_at.hour`, and `can_bid` looks up `now.hour` from `request.received_at`. The day file is chosen by `served_at.date()`. If impressions and requests carry different tzinfo (or naive vs aware), the hour and day buckets will not line up and the hourly cap will be applied to the wrong bucket. Also `fromisoformat` can yield naive/aware mismatches.
findings.suggestion: Normalise all timestamps to one timezone (e.g. UTC) before deriving date/hour.

findings.title: Invalid marker is keyed only by impression id and lacks campaign
findings.description: mark_invalid writes {"kind":"invalid","id":...} to the day file of served_at. If the impression was served in a different timezone or its served_at is naive/aware inconsistently, the date may differ from the one used at append, so the marker lands in a different file and for_day never sees it. Refunds then silently have no effect. Also, repeated refunds are not idempotent in the file, though harmless on read.
findings.suggestion: Ensure the same day derivation is used for append and mark_invalid (e.g. normalise to UTC), and consider validating that the original record exists.

findings.title: Whole day file re-read and parsed for every campaign on every bid
findings.description: The pacer previously kept in-memory spend. Now can_bid calls spend(), which calls for_day, which re-reads and JSON-parses the entire day file, for each campaign on each bid request (eligible loops over all campaigns). Cost is O(requests x campaigns x impressions in the day), growing through the day; the report does the same per campaign. This will become very slow on the hot bid path.
findings.suggestion: Cache per-day, per-campaign spend in memory (updated on record/refund) or index the log; avoid re-reading the file on each bid.

findings.title: Hourly bucket uses impression's own timezone hour, not the request's
findings.description: Impressions are bucketed by impression.served_at.hour, while the cap check uses now.hour from request.received_at. If the datetimes carry different tzinfo (or one is naive), buckets mismatch and the hourly cap is applied to the wrong hour. Also day files are chosen by served_at.date() in its own timezone.
findings.suggestion: Normalise all datetimes to one timezone before deriving date and hour.

findings.title: Invalid marker keyed only by impression id is dropped if the impression's day differs
findings.description: mark_invalid writes the marker to the file for impression.served_at.date(), and for_day reads only that day's file, so this works only if the caller passes an impression with the same served_at as the original. A caller that builds the refund impression with a different served_at (e.g. timezone differences, or the date derived from a different datetime) writes the marker to another day's file, and the original impression keeps counting against the budget. Also, if the original append was never written in this file, the marker is silently orphaned.
findings.suggestion: Validate that the impression exists, or store the day in the marker and look markers up from the original impression's file.

findings.title: Whole day file re-read and parsed for every campaign on every bid check
findings.description: Spend was previously kept in memory. can_bid now calls spend(), which calls for_day(), which opens and parses the full day's JSONL file for every campaign on each bid request. eligible() therefore reads the file once per campaign per request, and the cost grows with the day's impression volume, which hurts latency on the hot path.
findings.suggestion: Cache per-day spend in memory, updated on record/refund, or index the log by campaign.

findings.title: Bundle.locale is now the normalised locale, not the one requested
findings.description: The bundle is built with locale=chain[0], which is the normalised tag. A caller passing 'pt_br' or 'PT-br' gets a bundle whose locale is 'pt-BR'. Previously the locale was returned as given. Callers that key bundles or reports by the requested string (e.g. missing_report) can now see a different key than the one they passed.
findings.suggestion: Keep the requested locale in Bundle.locale, and use the normalised chain only for lookups. Or document and test the change.

findings.title: Per-key exists/get calls replace the single batched get_many lookup
findings.description: The previous code made one catalog.get_many call for all keys. The new code calls catalog.exists and catalog.get for every key in every candidate locale, so a page with N keys and a chain of length L makes up to 2*N*L catalog calls. If the catalog is backed by a DB or file, this becomes an N+1 pattern. The two calls per hit are also not atomic.
findings.suggestion: Fetch with get_many per locale in the chain for the keys still unresolved, and shrink the unresolved set after each locale.

findings.title: Per-key catalog lookups replace the batched get_many call
findings.description: The old code fetched all keys with one catalog.get_many(locale, wanted). The new loop calls catalog.exists and then catalog.get for every key in every locale of the chain. That is up to 2 * keys * chain-length calls. If the catalog is backed by a DB or file, this becomes an N+1 pattern, and the two calls per key are also not atomic.
findings.suggestion: Use catalog.get_many per locale in the chain, only for the keys still unresolved, so the number of calls is bounded by the chain length.

findings.title: Bundle locale is normalised, which breaks the fallback_keys comparison and callers
findings.description: Bundle.locale is set to chain[0], the normalised tag (for example pt_br becomes pt-BR), not the locale the caller passed in. Callers and missing_report that key on the requested locale string now get a different value. A catalog that stores non-canonical names, such as pt_BR, will also never match the normalised candidates, so every key is reported missing.
findings.suggestion: Keep the caller's requested locale in Bundle.locale, or ensure the catalog is queried with matching keys. Compare sources against the normalised chain[0] consistently.

findings.title: Per-key catalog lookups replace the batched get_many call
findings.description: The old code fetched all keys with a single catalog.get_many(locale, wanted) call. The new loop calls catalog.exists and then catalog.get for every key in every candidate locale, so a page with N keys and a chain of length L makes up to 2*N*L catalog calls. If the catalog is backed by a DB or file, this becomes an N+1 pattern, and exists followed by get is also a check-then-act race if the catalog is reloaded in between.
findings.suggestion: Call catalog.get_many(candidate, remaining_keys) once per locale in the chain, shrinking the set of remaining keys after each call.

findings.title: Bundle.locale is now the normalised locale instead of the requested one
findings.description: Bundle.locale is set to chain[0], which is the normalised tag (for example 'pt_br' becomes 'pt-BR'), rather than the caller's locale. Callers, serialised JSON and missing_report keys that rely on the original string will see a different value. Invalid or empty locales now raise ValueError from normalise, where they previously just yielded all-missing bundles.
findings.suggestion: Keep locale=locale in the Bundle, or normalise consistently and document the change. Compare sources against chain[0] inside fallback_keys.

findings.title: delete_entry authorizes with reader check instead of owner check
findings.description: delete_entry calls _require_reader, so any user the entry is shared with can permanently delete the owner's journal entry. Every other destructive or mutating handler (edit, share, unshare) uses _require_owner. Deletion by a mere reader causes data loss for the owner.
findings.suggestion: Use _require_owner(entry, user) in delete_entry. Readers should use leave_entry instead.

findings.title: delete_entry authorizes with reader check instead of owner check
findings.description: delete_entry calls _require_reader, so any user the entry is shared with can permanently delete the owner's journal entry. Every other destructive operation (edit, share, unshare) uses _require_owner. A reader can destroy data they should only be able to view or leave.
findings.suggestion: Use _require_owner(entry, user) in delete_entry.

findings.title: delete_entry authorizes with reader check instead of owner check
findings.description: delete_entry calls _require_reader, so any user the entry is shared with can permanently delete the owner's journal entry. Every other destructive or mutating operation (edit, share, unshare) uses _require_owner. Deleting is destructive and should be restricted to the owner.
findings.suggestion: Use _require_owner(entry, user) in delete_entry.

findings.title: Invite codes generated with non-cryptographic PRNG
findings.description: Invite codes are bearer secrets that grant workspace membership, but they are generated with `random.choices`, which uses the Mersenne Twister. Its output is predictable once enough outputs are observed, so an attacker who sees a few codes could predict others and join workspaces uninvited.
findings.suggestion: Use the `secrets` module, e.g. `"".join(secrets.choice(CODE_ALPHABET) for _ in range(CODE_LENGTH))`, or `secrets.token_urlsafe`.

findings.title: accept() does not check link expiry
findings.description: `accept` checks only `revoked` and `uses >= max_uses`. It ignores `expires_at`, which `is_active` does check. An expired link can therefore still be used to join a workspace, making the TTL meaningless.
findings.suggestion: Use `if not link.is_active(now): raise InviteNotUsable(...)`.

findings.title: Invite role is not re-validated and uses are consumed non-atomically
findings.description: `accept` creates the member and only then increments `link.uses`. The check and the increment are not atomic, so concurrent accepts of a single-use link can both pass the check and exceed `max_uses`. Separately, `accept` never checks that the link's creator is still a manager, so a link created by a since-demoted admin remains valid.
findings.suggestion: Guard check, add and increment with a lock, or increment before the add and roll back on failure. Optionally re-verify the creator's manager status.
