findings.description: Invite codes are bearer secrets that grant workspace membership, but they are generated with `random.choices`, which uses the Mersenne Twister. Its output is predictable once enough outputs are observed. An attacker who sees a few codes can predict others and join workspaces uninvited.
findings.suggestion: Use the `secrets` module, e.g. `"".join(secrets.choice(CODE_ALPHABET) for _ in range(CODE_LENGTH))`, or `secrets.token_urlsafe`.

findings.title: accept() does not check link expiry
findings.description: `accept` rejects revoked or exhausted links but never checks `expires_at`. It does not call `is_active(now)`. An expired link can still be used to join the workspace, which defeats the TTL.
findings.suggestion: Use `if not link.is_active(now): raise InviteNotUsable(...)`.

findings.title: Link creator can revoke without being a manager any more
findings.description: If the actor created the link, the manager check is skipped. A creator who has since been demoted or removed from the workspace can still revoke the link. It would be safer to require current manager status, or at least membership, for everyone.
findings.suggestion: Always call `require_manager`, or at minimum check current membership for the creator.

findings.title: Link role can exceed what the creator may now grant, and accept uses stored role unchecked
findings.description: `accept` adds the user with `link.role` without re-checking that the creator is still a manager. A link created by an admin who was later demoted or removed keeps granting ADMIN access to new members.
findings.suggestion: On accept, verify that `link.created_by` is still a manager in the workspace, or revoke the creator's links when their role changes.

Its output is predictable once enough outputs are observed, so an attacker who sees a few codes could predict others and join workspaces uninvited.
findings.suggestion: Use the `secrets` module, e.g. `"".join(secrets.choice(CODE_ALPHABET) for _ in range(CODE_LENGTH))`, or `secrets.token_urlsafe`.

findings.title: accept() ignores link expiry
findings.description: `accept` checks only `revoked` and `uses`, not `expires_at`. `is_active` checks expiry, but `accept` does not use it, so expired links can still be used to join a workspace. The TTL is effectively unenforced.
findings.suggestion: Use `if not link.is_active(now): raise InviteNotUsable(...)`.

findings.title: comp_tickets only requires login, not a staff/admin role
findings.description: Any logged-in attendee can call tickets.comp and issue free tickets (price 0) to any holder, up to 50 per request. Other privileged routes (event.cancel, event.attendees) use require_role. This lets any user bypass payment entirely.
findings.suggestion: Call require_role(request.user, Role.STAFF, Role.ADMIN) and use the returned user for issued_by.

findings.title: comp_tickets lacks role check; any logged-in user can issue free tickets
findings.description: comp_tickets only calls require_login. Any authenticated attendee can issue up to 50 free tickets per request to any holder, so they can bypass payment entirely. Other privileged routes (cancel_event, attendee_list) use require_role.
findings.suggestion: Call require_role(request.user, Role.STAFF, Role.ADMIN) (or ADMIN only) and use the returned user for issued_by.

findings.title: Complimentary ticket endpoint lacks role authorization
findings.description: comp_tickets only calls require_login, so any logged-in attendee can issue up to 50 free tickets per request to any holder. Other privileged handlers (cancel_event, attendee_list) use require_role. Anyone can drain event capacity and bypass payment.
findings.suggestion: Call require_role(request.user, Role.STAFF, Role.ADMIN) (or ADMIN) instead of require_login, then use the returned user for issued_by.

findings.title: move_card does not check permission on the source board
findings.description: The card is fetched and only the destination board is checked with _require_editor. Any user who is an editor on their own board can pass any card_id from a board they have no access to and move it into their board. That leaks and steals the card, and it also shifts positions of cards in the victim's column through detach. Nothing checks the actor's role on card.board_id.
findings.suggestion: Call self._require_editor(card.board_id, actor_id) before moving, in addition to the check on the target board.

findings.title: Archived card keeps its stale position, and unarchive/move behavior is inconsistent
findings.description: archive_card calls detach and then sets archived=True but leaves card.position unchanged. Archived cards are filtered out of cards_in_column, so any later restore would collide with live positions. Because the check order in move_card also reports errors differently, state may become inconsistent.
findings.suggestion: Reset the position on archive, or re-insert the card when it is restored, so positions stay contiguous.

findings.title: move_card does not check permission on the source board
findings.description: Only editor rights on the destination board are checked. The card is looked up by id and nothing verifies that the actor can edit (or even view) the card's current board. A user who is an editor of their own board can pass any card_id from a private board and move it into their board. This steals the card, leaks its contents, and removes it from the victim board.
findings.suggestion: Call self._require_editor(card.board_id, actor_id) for the source board before checking the target board.

findings.title: Moving a card within the same column corrupts positions
findings.description: detach() decrements the positions of cards below the card, but card.position is left unchanged. insert() then excludes the card and shifts others with position >= target. The stale position no longer matches the compacted order. Moving within the same column therefore produces gaps or duplicate positions, and an unrelated card can end up out of order. In addition, the move is not atomic.
findings.suggestion: Compute the position after detaching, or reorder the column as a list and renumber all positions 0..n-1.

findings.title: Archived card keeps its stale position
findings.description: Archiving detaches the card, which closes the gap for the others, but card.position stays at its old value. Nothing resets it, and no unarchive path exists yet. Any later restore would reuse a stale position and collide with other cards.
findings.suggestion: Reset position (for example to 0 or None) on archive, or re-insert the card when it is unarchived.

findings.title: move_card does not check permission on the card's source board
findings.description: Only the target board is checked with _require_editor. The card is fetched by id and moved without verifying the actor can edit the card's current board. A user who is an editor on their own board can pass any card_id from a private board they have no access to, and the card is moved onto their board. This lets them take cards from other boards and read them afterwards. Any viewer or non-member of the source board can also move cards out of it.
findings.suggestion: Call self._require_editor(card.board_id, actor_id) for the source board before moving, in addition to the target check.

findings.title: Partner domain match uses endswith without a dot boundary
findings.description: `host.endswith(domain)` accepts any host whose name merely ends with the partner domain string. With partner domain `shop.example`, an attacker-registered host such as `evilshop.example` or `notshop.example` passes. The policy then reflects that origin with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, so the attacker's page can read member balances and redeem rewards using the victim's session cookie.
findings.suggestion: Require an exact match or a subdomain boundary: `host == domain or host.endswith('.' + domain)`.

findings.title: Origin with userinfo or port is not validated
findings.description: For the partner check only the scheme, hostname, path and query are validated. An origin like `https://user@shop.example` or one with an arbitrary port is accepted and reflected verbatim in Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Real browser Origin headers never contain userinfo, so such values only come from non-browser clients. Reflecting unvalidated text makes the check looser than intended.
findings.suggestion: Reject origins where `parts.username` or `parts.password` is set, and decide explicitly whether to allow a port. Alternatively, compare against a rebuilt `https://hostname[:port]` string.

findings.title: Partner domain suffix match lacks a dot boundary, allowing attacker origins with credentials
findings.description: `host.endswith(domain)` matches any host that merely ends with the partner domain string. With partner domain `shop.example`, the origin `https://evilshop.example` or `https://attacker-shop.example` passes. The policy then reflects the origin with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, so an attacker-registered domain can read members' balances and redeem rewards using their session cookies. The apex domain itself is also matched, which may or may not be intended.
findings.suggestion: Require an exact match or a dot boundary: `host == domain or host.endswith('.' + domain)`.

findings.title: Ports and userinfo not validated in partner-origin check
findings.description: The check uses `parts.hostname`, which drops the port and userinfo. Origins such as `https://x.shop.example:8443` are allowed on any port, and a malformed origin containing userinfo can pass the check. The unmodified (non-normalised) origin is then echoed back in the response headers.
findings.suggestion: Validate `parts.netloc` against the hostname (reject userinfo), and decide explicitly whether ports are permitted.

findings.title: Partner domain check uses bare endswith, allowing look-alike origins with credentials
findings.description: `host.endswith(domain)` does not require a dot boundary. With partner domain `shop.example`, an attacker-controlled origin like `https://evilshop.example` or `https://notshop.example` passes. The API then reflects that origin with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, so the attacker's site can read member balances and redeem rewards using the victim's session cookie.
findings.suggestion: Accept only `host == domain` or `host.endswith('.' + domain)`.

findings.title: Allow-Origin echoes the raw origin rather than the normalised one
findings.description: The header reflects the request's original `origin` string. A trailing slash is stripped for the allow check but is still echoed back, so a request with `Origin: https://a.example/` gets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://a.example/`. Browsers compare this to the serialized origin, which has no trailing slash, so the request would be blocked. The same applies to the preflight response at line 63.
findings.suggestion: Return the normalised origin, or the exact configured origin, in the header.

findings.title: Connection leaked and not rolled back on non-InventoryError exceptions
findings.description: In reserve(), release is called after the try/except rather than in a finally block. On the InventoryError path the code re-raises, so release is skipped and the connection is never returned to the pool. Any other exception (e.g. a DB error from put/commit) is not caught, so there is no rollback and no release either. Repeated failures such as insufficient stock will exhaust the pool.
findings.suggestion: Use try/except/finally: roll back on any exception (except Exception: conn.rollback(); raise) and call self._pool.release(conn) in a finally block.

findings.title: Check-then-act on stock without locking allows overselling
findings.description: reserve() reads the row, checks free stock, then writes it back with no row lock or version check. Two concurrent reservations for the same SKU can both read the same free value and both succeed, so reserved exceeds on_hand. The same lost-update race affects cancel() and receive() read-modify-write.
findings.suggestion: Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or an atomic conditional update, or optimistic versioning, within the transaction.

findings.title: cancel() has no rollback and can crash on missing SKU row
findings.description: If conn.get returns None for a SKU, row['reserved'] raises TypeError after earlier lines have already been modified via put. No rollback is done before the connection is released, so the partial changes may remain pending on the pooled connection and be committed later by another user.
findings.suggestion: Roll back on any exception before release, and handle a missing stock row explicitly.

findings.title: Duplicate SKUs in lines can bypass the free check
findings.description: If lines contains the same SKU twice, the row is re-read per line, so this is fine only if conn.get returns fresh copies of uncommitted writes. If get reads from committed state, the second line sees stale reserved and overwrites the first increment, so reserved is under-counted while the reservation records both quantities. Cancel then subtracts both, driving reserved negative.
findings.suggestion: Aggregate quantities per SKU before checking and updating.

findings.title: Connection leaked and not rolled back on non-InventoryError exceptions
findings.description: In reserve(), the release call sits after the try/except instead of in a finally block. On the error path the except clause re-raises, so release is skipped and the connection leaks. Any other exception (e.g. a DB error from conn.put/commit) skips both rollback and release. Repeated failures such as InsufficientStock exhaust the pool. The connection may also be left with uncommitted partial changes.
findings.suggestion: Use try/except/finally: roll back on any exception (except Exception: conn.rollback(); raise) and call self._pool.release(conn) in a finally block.

findings.title: Duplicate SKUs in lines are checked against stale row
findings.description: If the same SKU appears in several lines, each iteration re-reads the row. This works only if conn.get returns the pending written value. With a read-committed or cached get that returns a fresh copy, the second line may overwrite the first reservation. The combined quantity is also never checked against free stock when the lines are validated separately.
findings.suggestion: Aggregate quantities per SKU before checking and reserving.

findings.title: cancel lacks rollback and crashes on missing stock row
findings.description: If a SKU row is missing, conn.get returns None and row['reserved'] raises TypeError midway. Earlier puts are not rolled back before the connection is released to the pool, so partial changes may leak into later use of that connection.
findings.suggestion: Handle a missing row, and call conn.rollback() on any exception before releasing.

findings.title: Connection leaked and not rolled back on non-InventoryError exceptions
findings.description: In reserve(), release() is called only on the success path after the try/except. If InventoryError is raised, the handler re-raises and release() on line 96 is skipped, leaking the pooled connection on every failed reservation (insufficient stock, unknown SKU, duplicate). Other exceptions (DB errors) skip both rollback and release. The pool will be exhausted under normal failure traffic.
findings.suggestion: Use try/except/finally: roll back on any exception (`except Exception: conn.rollback(); raise`) and call self._pool.release(conn) in a finally block.

findings.title: Duplicate SKUs in lines can over-reserve or depend on mutable row aliasing
findings.description: Each line re-reads the stock row and checks free stock independently. If the same SKU appears in multiple lines, the result depends on whether conn.get returns a fresh copy or shared object. With copies and uncommitted puts not visible, the second line's free check ignores the first line's reservation, which could over-reserve. Also the check-then-write is not locked, so concurrent reserves can oversell.
findings.suggestion: Aggregate quantities per SKU before checking, and read stock rows with a lock (e.g. SELECT FOR UPDATE) within the transaction.

findings.title: cancel has no rollback and assumes the stock row exists
findings.description: If a stock row is missing, row is None and `row['reserved']` raises TypeError mid-loop after earlier puts, with no rollback before the connection is released to the pool, leaving partial uncommitted changes on a reused connection.
findings.suggestion: Add rollback on exception before releasing, and handle a missing row explicitly.

findings.title: Temp upload file leaked when blob already exists
findings.description: When the target already exists, the function returns early without removing the temporary file at `incoming`. Every duplicate upload leaves a full-size `upload-<uuid>` file in `incoming/`, so disk usage grows without bound. The old code wrote no temp file in this case.
findings.suggestion: Call `incoming.unlink(missing_ok=True)` before returning on the duplicate path, and also clean up if `_path_for`, `mkdir` or `os.replace` raises.

findings.title: No cleanup of temp file if mkdir or replace fails
findings.description: The cleanup `try/except` covers only the write loop. If `target.parent.mkdir` or `os.replace` raises (permissions, disk error), the temp file stays in `incoming/` forever.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the finalize steps in a try/except that unlinks `incoming` on failure.

findings.title: Temp upload file leaked when blob already exists
findings.description: When the target already exists, the function returns early without removing the temporary file in incoming/. Every duplicate upload leaves a full-size orphan file, so disk usage grows without bound. The old code wrote nothing in this case.
findings.suggestion: Call incoming.unlink(missing_ok=True) before returning. Better, wrap the post-write section in try/finally that removes incoming if it was not moved.

findings.title: Temp file leaked if mkdir or os.replace fails
findings.description: The cleanup try/except covers only the write loop. If _path_for, target.parent.mkdir or os.replace raises (permissions, disk error), the temp file in incoming/ remains.
findings.suggestion: Extend the cleanup to cover the finalize steps, for example with try/finally that unlinks incoming if it still exists.

findings.title: Temp upload file leaked when blob already exists
findings.description: When the target already exists, the function returns early without removing the temp file in incoming/. Every duplicate upload leaves a full-size orphan file in the incoming directory, so disk usage grows without bound. The old code wrote nothing in this case.
findings.suggestion: Call incoming.unlink(missing_ok=True) before returning in the target.exists() branch. Also unlink the temp file if mkdir or os.replace raises, for example with try/finally.

findings.title: Temp file leaked if mkdir or replace fails after the write
findings.description: The cleanup try/except covers only the write phase. If _path_for, target.parent.mkdir or os.replace raises, for example on a permission error or a full disk, the temp file in incoming/ stays behind.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the post-write steps in try/except or try/finally that unlinks the temp file on failure.

findings.title: Capacity check counts countries instead of entries
findings.description: The eviction loop compares len(self._keys_by_country), the number of distinct countries, with max_entries. The number of cached rates is len(self._entries). The cache therefore never evicts until there are more than max_entries countries, so it grows without bound by postal code. The old lru_cache(maxsize=4096) capped the number of rates, so this removes that bound.
findings.suggestion: Use `while len(self._entries) > self._max_entries:`.

findings.title: clear() does not reset stats while invalidate_country also ignores bookkeeping consistency
findings.description: Entries expire by TTL but are never removed from _entries or _keys_by_country when they are replaced. The expired key is re-stored, which is harmless for the set. However, `_evict_oldest` and `invalidate_country` assume the indexes stay in sync. `invalidate_country` does `del self._entries[key]`, which raises KeyError if a key was already evicted. This is currently guarded because eviction removes the key from the set, but the capacity-check bug above leaves the eviction path wrongly gated.
findings.suggestion: Use `self._entries.pop(key, None)` in invalidate_country to be robust.

findings.title: Table replaced before cache invalidation; stale rate can be cached in between
findings.description: put_country_rates replaces the table and only then invalidates the cache. A concurrent lookup in the gap can still be served the old cached rate. A lookup that misses can load a rate and store it either side of the replace, so it may cache a rate from the old table after the invalidation if it started before. The class docstring claims the lock rules this out, but replace_country is not performed under the cache lock.
findings.suggestion: Perform the replace and the invalidation atomically, for example by running the table swap while holding the cache lock.

findings.title: Distinct prefixes can collapse after normalisation and silently overwrite each other
findings.description: Normalising keys can map different input prefixes (e.g. 'ab 1' and 'AB1') to the same key. The later entry silently overwrites the earlier one, which may have a different rate, and no error is reported.
findings.suggestion: Detect duplicate normalised keys and return a 400.

findings.title: Eviction bound checks number of countries instead of number of entries
findings.description: The loop compares len(self._keys_by_country), the number of distinct countries, with max_entries. The cache therefore only evicts once there are more countries than max_entries, so it can hold unlimited entries per country, and the limit is effectively never enforced. Memory grows without bound as new postal codes are seen, within the TTL. The `evictions` metric will also stay at 0.
findings.suggestion: Use `while len(self._entries) > self._max_entries:`.

findings.title: clear() does not reset or account for stats
findings.description: clear() drops entries without counting them as evictions or invalidations. Stats remain consistent only loosely, which may mislead metrics. This is minor.

findings.title: Expired entry replaced without cleaning country index consistency
findings.description: When an expired entry is reloaded, the key is re-added to the set, which is fine. However, if the loader raises (UnknownJurisdiction), the stale expired entry stays in the cache and counts toward size. It is also still counted as a miss. Expired entries are never purged except by LRU, so they occupy slots.
findings.suggestion: Delete the expired entry (and its index entry) before calling the loader.

findings.title: Capacity check counts countries instead of entries
findings.description: The eviction loop compares len(self._keys_by_country), the number of distinct countries, with max_entries, not the number of cached entries. The cache therefore grows without bound: with 4096 as the limit, millions of postal codes within a few countries are never evicted. Memory use is unbounded, and the max_entries guarantee in the docstring is broken. The stats 'size' and 'evictions' are also misleading as a result.
findings.suggestion: Use `while len(self._entries) > self._max_entries:`.

findings.title: clear() does not reset statistics
findings.description: clear() empties the entries and the country index but leaves the hit, miss and eviction counters unchanged. This is a minor inconsistency, and it is arguably intentional.

findings.title: Table replacement and cache invalidation are not atomic
findings.description: source.replace_country runs before calculator.rates_changed and without the cache lock. A concurrent get() can load the old or new table between the two calls, and the loader does not run under any lock shared with the source. A lookup that loads the new rate is harmless. A lookup that has just read the old table, however, can store the stale rate after the invalidation has run. That stale rate then stays cached for up to the TTL.
findings.suggestion: Do the replace and the invalidate under a single lock shared with the cache loader, or invalidate again after the replace.

findings.title: Counting lines consumes a one-shot iterator, so nothing is processed
findings.description: `total = sum(1 for _ in lines)` exhausts `lines` before the main loop runs. The CLI passes an open file object, which is a one-shot iterator. The `for line in lines` loop then sees no lines, so read/written stay 0 and the output file is empty. Progress reports 0/total.
findings.suggestion: Avoid the pre-count (report progress without a total), or materialise the lines in a list, or count in a separate pass that reopens or seeks the file.

findings.title: Retry returns an un-awaited coroutine instead of the Event
findings.description: In the `except LookupTimeout` branch the code does `return enrich(event, geo)` without `await`. `enrich_one` therefore returns a coroutine object, which `_flush` passes to `sink`. `to_json` then fails or writes garbage, and the coroutine is never awaited. The retry never actually runs. A second timeout would not abort the run as documented.
findings.suggestion: Use `return await enrich(event, geo)` so the retry runs and a second LookupTimeout propagates.

findings.title: Failure in one lookup leaves sibling tasks running and the batch partially handled
findings.description: `asyncio.gather` without handling leaves the other tasks running when one raises, so they may continue after the exception propagates. Because the sink is only called after the whole batch completes, a failure discards that batch's results. Earlier batches are already written, so the output file is left partially written.
findings.suggestion: Use `asyncio.TaskGroup`, or cancel the pending tasks on error.

findings.title: Counting lines consumes a one-shot iterator, so nothing is processed
findings.description: `total = sum(1 for _ in lines)` iterates the whole `lines` iterable. The CLI passes an open file object, which is a one-shot iterator. After the count it is exhausted, so the `for line in lines` loop at line 54 sees no lines. The output is empty and stats.read is 0, while progress reports 0/total.
findings.suggestion: Avoid the pre-pass: pass total as an optional argument, or materialize the lines into a list (at the cost of memory), or seek the file back to the start. Alternatively drop the total from the progress callback.

findings.title: Retry returns an un-awaited coroutine instead of the Event
findings.description: In the except branch, `return enrich(event, geo)` is missing `await`. enrich_one therefore returns a coroutine object. The retry never runs inside the semaphore, a second LookupTimeout is never raised in this task so it cannot abort the run as documented, and `sink` receives a coroutine rather than an Event. `to_json` then fails or writes garbage, and a 'coroutine was never awaited' warning appears.
findings.suggestion: Use `return await enrich(event, geo)` so the retry runs under the semaphore and a second timeout propagates.

findings.title: Retry returns un-awaited coroutine instead of an Event
findings.description: On LookupTimeout the handler does `return enrich(event, geo)` without `await`. enrich is now async, so enrich_one returns a coroutine object. gather puts it in the results, and sink(event) then calls to_json on a coroutine, which crashes or writes garbage. The retry never runs, and a second timeout is never raised, contrary to the docstring. It also emits a 'never awaited' warning.
findings.suggestion: Use `return await enrich(event, geo)` in the except block, so a second LookupTimeout propagates and aborts the run.

findings.title: Input iterable consumed to count total, so the processing loop sees nothing
findings.description: `total = sum(1 for _ in lines)` iterates `lines` fully. The CLI passes a file object, which is a one-shot iterator and is now exhausted. The following `for line in lines` reads nothing, so no events are processed. The output is empty, stats.read is 0, and progress shows 0/total. Any generator input behaves the same way.
findings.suggestion: Do not pre-count the input. Report progress by bytes read, or materialize the lines into a list first (memory cost), or have the caller seek the file back to the start.
